name: CBSE Class 10 Maths
fullName: CBSE Class X Board Examination – Mathematics (Standard) – Objective Practice
frequency: Twice a year from 2026: main exam (Feb–Mar, compulsory) + optional second exam (May)
eligibility: Class 10 students of CBSE-affiliated schools (regular and private candidates as per CBSE rules)

notification.summary: For the 2026-27 session, CBSE released the sample question papers and marking schemes (Mathematics Standard and Basic) in late September 2026 on cbseacademic.nic.in; the question-paper design is unchanged from 2025-26. The 2027 date sheet had not been issued as of 10 Oct 2026 and is expected in the second half of October. Under the two-exam system, the main (first) board exam is expected from mid-February 2027 and the optional second exam in May 2027.

pattern.stage: Board Theory Paper – Section A (objective part only)
pattern.notes: This mock simulates ONLY the objective Section A of the 80-mark, 3-hour theory paper: 18 MCQs plus 2 Assertion-Reason questions of 1 mark each. Sections B–E (VSA, SA, LA and case-based questions, 60 marks) and the 20-mark internal assessment are not simulated. The question count per unit is scaled from the unit weightage (Number Systems 6, Algebra 20, Coordinate Geometry 6, Geometry 15, Trigonometry 12, Mensuration 10, Statistics & Probability 11 marks). Questions follow the rationalised NCERT syllabus (Mathematics Standard). There is no negative marking.

trendAnalysis.summary: Based on the 2024 and 2025 board papers, the 2026 main exam and the CBSE sample papers. The paper design has been stable since 2023-24: 20 one-mark questions in Section A (including 2 Assertion-Reason), with about 50% competency-based questions across the paper. Algebra (quadratics, AP, linear equations) carries the most weight. Section A MCQs are mostly direct and formula-based (HCF/LCM, zeroes of a polynomial, discriminant, trigonometric values, probability, mean/mode relation), with a few tricky ones from triangles and circles. The 2026-27 sample paper keeps the same design, with slightly more application-based MCQs. Overall Section A difficulty is easy to moderate.

resources.notes: CBSE publishes sample question papers with marking schemes each session on cbseacademic.nic.in, and previous years' question papers and marking schemes on cbse.gov.in (Question Papers section). The Competency Focused Questions bank is also on cbseacademic.nic.in.

questions.question: Which of the following is an irrational number?
questions.explanation: √12 = 2√3 is irrational. √16 = 4, 0.75 = 3/4 and 22/7 are rational.

relevance.note: Pick irrational among surd/rationals; CBSE Section A MCQ style

questions.topic: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, HCF & LCM
questions.question: For every natural number n, the number 6ⁿ ends with the digit:
questions.explanation: 6 × 6 = 36 ends in 6, and multiplying any number ending in 6 by 6 again gives a last digit of 6. (It can never end in 0, because 6ⁿ has no factor 5.)

relevance.note: Last digit of 6^n; MCQ twist on NCERT 'can 6^n end in 0' rather than a copy

questions.question: The sum of the zeroes of the polynomial 2x² − 8x + 6 is:
questions.explanation: Sum of zeroes = −b/a = −(−8)/2 = 4. (The product is c/a = 3.)

relevance.note: Sum of zeroes -b/a = 4 with sign trap; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: A quadratic polynomial whose zeroes are 3 and −5 is:
questions.explanation: Sum = −2 and product = −15, so the polynomial is x² − (sum)x + product = x² + 2x − 15.

relevance.note: Quadratic from zeroes with sign-swap traps; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: If 2 is a zero of the polynomial x² − kx + 6, the value of k is:
questions.explanation: Substitute x = 2: 4 − 2k + 6 = 0 ⇒ k = 5.

relevance.note: k from given zero = 5 with sign trap; CBSE MCQ

questions.topic: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
questions.question: The pair of equations 2x + 3y = 7 and 4x + 6y = 14 has:
questions.explanation: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ = 1/2, so the lines coincide and there are infinitely many solutions.

relevance.note: Proportional coefficients -> infinitely many; CBSE consistency MCQ

questions.topic: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
questions.question: The pair of equations kx + 2y = 5 and 3x + y = 1 has a unique solution when:
questions.explanation: A unique solution needs a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂: k/3 ≠ 2/1 ⇒ k ≠ 6.

relevance.note: Unique solution k≠6 with k=6 trap; frequent CBSE MCQ

questions.topic: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
questions.question: The lines represented by 3x − y = 4 and 6x − 2y = 9 are:
questions.explanation: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = 1/2 but c₁/c₂ = 4/9 ≠ 1/2, so the lines are parallel (no solution).

relevance.note: Ratios 1/2,1/2,4/9 -> parallel; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The discriminant of the quadratic equation 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0 is:

relevance.note: Discriminant -8 with sign traps; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The roots of x² + 4x + 4 = 0 are:
questions.explanation: D = 16 − 16 = 0, so the roots are real and equal (both −2).

relevance.note: Perfect square -> real and equal roots; CBSE nature-of-roots MCQ

questions.question: The positive value of k for which x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots is:
questions.explanation: Equal roots ⇒ k² − 36 = 0 ⇒ k = ±6; the positive value is 6.

relevance.note: Equal roots k^2=36 -> 6 with 3/9/18 traps; CBSE favourite

questions.question: The 10th term of the AP 2, 7, 12, … is:

relevance.note: a10 = 47 with 52 (n instead of n-1) trap; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The sum of the first 15 terms of the AP 3, 7, 11, … is:

relevance.note: S15 = 465; CBSE AP sum MCQ

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The 11th term of the AP 7, 4, 1, … is −23.
Reason (R): The nth term of an AP with first term a and common difference d is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation: R is the standard formula and is true. Using it: a₁₁ = 7 + 10(−3) = −23, so A is true and follows from R.

relevance.note: A-R on AP nth term, both true and R explains; CBSE A-R format

questions.question: The distance of the point (−6, 8) from the origin is:

relevance.note: Distance from origin 10 with 14/100 traps

questions.question: The point that divides the line segment joining (1, 2) and (7, 8) internally in the ratio 1 : 2 is:

relevance.note: Section formula 1:2 -> (3,4) with 2:1 trap (5,6)

questions.question: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. If AD = 3 cm, DB = 2 cm and AE = 4.5 cm, then EC is:
questions.explanation: By BPT, AD/DB = AE/EC ⇒ 3/2 = 4.5/EC ⇒ EC = 3 cm.

relevance.note: BPT EC=3; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: ΔABC ~ ΔPQR and AB/PQ = 2/3. If BC = 8 cm, then QR is:
questions.explanation: Corresponding sides are proportional: BC/QR = 2/3 ⇒ QR = 8 × 3/2 = 12 cm.

relevance.note: Similar triangles QR=12 with inverted 16/3 trap

questions.question: In ΔABC, D and E lie on AB and AC with DE ∥ BC. If AD/DB = 3/5, then AE/AC is:
questions.explanation: By BPT, AE/EC = 3/5, so AE/AC = 3/(3 + 5) = 3/8.

relevance.note: AD/DB=3/5 -> AE/AC=3/8 with 3/5 trap; good CBSE MCQ

questions.question: From a point 13 cm away from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm, the length of the tangent is:
questions.explanation: The radius is perpendicular to the tangent: length = √(13² − 5²) = √144 = 12 cm.

relevance.note: Tangent length 12 via 5-12-13; CBSE MCQ with fresh numbers

questions.question: PA and PB are tangents from an external point P to a circle with centre O. If ∠APB = 70°, then ∠AOB is:
questions.explanation: In quadrilateral OAPB, ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°, so ∠AOB = 360° − 180° − 70° = 110°.

relevance.note: ∠AOB = 180-70 = 110° with 140 trap; CBSE MCQ

questions.question:
Assertion (A): For any given line, a circle has exactly two tangents parallel to that line.
Reason (R): From a point outside a circle, exactly two tangents can be drawn to it.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation: A is true: the tangents parallel to a given direction touch the circle at the two ends of the diameter perpendicular to that direction. R is also true, but it is about tangents through one external point, not parallel tangents, so R does not explain A.

relevance.note: Both true but R does not explain A; good CBSE A-R item

questions.question: If tan θ = 3/4 and θ is acute, then sin θ is:
questions.explanation: Take opposite = 3, adjacent = 4; hypotenuse = 5. sin θ = 3/5.

relevance.note: tan 3/4 -> sin 3/5 with cos 4/5 trap

questions.question: (1 − sin²θ) sec²θ is equal to:
questions.explanation: 1 − sin²θ = cos²θ, and cos²θ × sec²θ = 1.

relevance.note: (1-sin^2)sec^2 = 1; CBSE identity MCQ

questions.question: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 20 m away from its foot on level ground is 60°. The height of the tower is:

relevance.note: Height = 20 tan60 = 20√3 with 20/√3 trap; CBSE heights MCQ

questions.question: A 10 m long ladder leans against a vertical wall and makes an angle of 60° with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?

relevance.note: Ladder 10 sin60 = 5√3 with cos trap; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The area of a sector of a circle of radius 6 cm with central angle 60° is:

relevance.note: Sector area 6π with full-circle/arc traps; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The length of an arc of a circle of radius 21 cm that subtends an angle of 60° at the centre is (π = 22/7):

relevance.note: Arc length 22 cm with 44 (diameter) trap

questions.question: The area of a quadrant of a circle of radius 14 cm is (π = 22/7):
questions.explanation: Quadrant area = ¼ × 22/7 × 14 × 14 = ¼ × 616 = 154 cm².

relevance.note: Quadrant area 154; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The curved surface area of a cone with base radius 7 cm and slant height 10 cm is (π = 22/7):
questions.explanation: CSA = πrl = 22/7 × 7 × 10 = 220 cm². (374 cm² would be the total surface area.)

relevance.note: Cone CSA πrl = 220 with TSA 374 trap

questions.question: The volume of a solid hemisphere of radius 3 cm is:

relevance.note: Hemisphere volume 18π with sphere 36π trap

questions.topic: Statistics (Mean, Median, Mode of Grouped Data)
questions.question: For a distribution, the mean is 20 and the median is 24. Using the empirical relation, the mode is:
questions.explanation: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean = 72 − 40 = 32.

relevance.note: Mode = 3×24 - 2×20 = 32; CBSE empirical-relation MCQ

questions.topic: Statistics (Mean, Median, Mode of Grouped Data)
questions.question: The values 5, 10 and 15 occur with frequencies 2, 3 and 5 respectively. The mean is:

relevance.note: Weighted mean 11.5 with unweighted 10 trap

questions.question: A fair die is thrown once. The probability of getting a number greater than 4 is:
questions.explanation: Favourable outcomes are {5, 6}: 2 out of 6, so the probability is 1/3.

relevance.note: P(>4) = 2/6 = 1/3 with ≥4 trap 1/2; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: Two coins are tossed together. The probability of getting at least one head is:
questions.explanation: Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. Three of the four have at least one head, so the probability is 3/4.

relevance.note: At least one head 3/4 with 1/2,1/4 traps; CBSE MCQ

questions.topic: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, HCF & LCM
questions.question: The HCF of two numbers is 12 and their product is 4320. Their LCM is:
questions.explanation: HCF × LCM = product of the numbers ⇒ LCM = 4320 ÷ 12 = 360.

relevance.note: LCM = 4320/12 = 360; CBSE HCF×LCM MCQ with fresh numbers

questions.topic: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, HCF & LCM
questions.question: If a = p³q² and b = p²q⁴, where p and q are distinct prime numbers, then HCF(a, b) is:
questions.explanation: HCF takes the smallest power of each common prime: p² and q², so HCF = p²q². (p³q⁴ is the LCM.)

relevance.note: HCF of p³q², p²q⁴ = p²q² with LCM trap; CBSE SQP-style

questions.topic: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, HCF & LCM
questions.question: The LCM of 2³ × 3² and 2² × 3³ is:
questions.explanation: LCM takes the greatest power of each prime: 2³ and 3³. (2² × 3² is the HCF.)

relevance.note: LCM of prime-power forms 2³×3³; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: Which of the following is an irrational number?
questions.explanation: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1, √49 = 7 and 22/7 are rational. 3 + 2√5 is irrational because √5 is irrational.

relevance.note: 3+2√5 irrational vs (2+√3)(2-√3)=1 trap; CBSE MCQ

questions.topic: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, HCF & LCM
questions.question:
Assertion (A): 6ⁿ ends with the digit 0 for some natural number n.
Reason (R): A natural number ends with the digit 0 if its prime factorisation contains both 2 and 5.

Choose the correct option.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation: R is true. But 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ has no factor 5, so it can never end in 0; A is false.

relevance.note: A-R: A false, R true on ending digit 0; CBSE A-R format

questions.question: If α and β are the zeroes of the polynomial x² − 6x + 8, then the value of α² + β² is:
questions.explanation: α + β = 6 and αβ = 8. α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 36 − 16 = 20.

relevance.note: α²+β² = 36-16 = 20 with 52 sign trap; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The product of the zeroes of the polynomial 3x² + 5x − 2 is:
questions.explanation: Product of zeroes = c/a = −2/3. (−5/3 is the sum of the zeroes.)

relevance.note: Product c/a = -2/3 with -b/a trap

questions.question: If 2 is a zero of the polynomial x² + 3x + k, then the value of k is:

relevance.note: k = -10 from zero 2; CBSE MCQ

questions.topic: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
questions.question: For what value of k does the pair of equations 2x + 3y = 5 and 4x + ky = 10 have infinitely many solutions?
questions.explanation: Infinitely many solutions need 2/4 = 3/k = 5/10. So 3/k = 1/2 ⇒ k = 6.

relevance.note: Infinitely many: k = 6; CBSE MCQ

questions.topic: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
questions.question: The pair of equations x + 2y = 4 and 2x + 4y = 12 represents two lines which are:
questions.explanation: a₁/a₂ = 1/2, b₁/b₂ = 2/4 = 1/2, c₁/c₂ = 4/12 = 1/3. Since a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂, the lines are parallel.

relevance.note: 1/2=2/4≠1/3 -> parallel; CBSE MCQ

questions.topic: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
questions.question: Five years ago, A was three times as old as B. Ten years from now, A will be twice as old as B. What is A's present age?

relevance.note: Age pair A=50, B=20; CBSE word-problem MCQ

questions.question: If x = 3 is a root of the equation x² − 2kx − 6 = 0, then the value of k is:

relevance.note: k = 1/2 from root 3; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The value of k for which the equation kx² − 6x + 1 = 0 has two equal roots is:
questions.explanation: Equal roots ⇒ D = 36 − 4k = 0 ⇒ k = 9.

relevance.note: Equal roots 36-4k=0 -> 9; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The 21st term of the AP 5, 9, 13, … is:
questions.explanation: a = 5, d = 4. a₂₁ = 5 + 20 × 4 = 85. (89 would be the 22nd term.)

relevance.note: a21 = 85 with 89 off-by-one trap

questions.question: The sum of the first 20 odd natural numbers is:
questions.explanation: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = 10 × (2 + 38) = 400. (In general, the sum of the first n odd numbers is n².)

relevance.note: Sum of first 20 odd numbers = 400; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The sum of the first n terms of an AP is given by Sₙ = 3n² + 2n. The common difference of the AP is:

relevance.note: d from Sₙ = 3n²+2n -> 6 with 3 trap; CBSE favourite

questions.question:
Assertion (A): −5, −5/2, 0, 5/2, … is an arithmetic progression.
Reason (R): The terms of an arithmetic progression cannot include both positive and negative numbers.

Choose the correct option.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation: The difference between consecutive terms is always 5/2, so A is true. An AP can contain both negative and positive terms (as this one does), so R is false.

relevance.note: A true (d=5/2), R false; CBSE A-R format with fresh claim

questions.question: If the distance between the points (4, p) and (1, 0) is 5 units, then the value of p is:

relevance.note: p = ±4 with 'only' traps; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: The ratio in which the x-axis divides the line segment joining the points (2, −3) and (5, 6) is:
questions.explanation: Let the ratio be k : 1. The y-coordinate of the point is (6k − 3)/(k + 1) = 0 ⇒ k = 1/2. Ratio = 1 : 2.

relevance.note: x-axis divides in 3:6 = 1:2; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: If (1, 2) is the mid-point of the line segment joining (a, 4) and (3, b), then:

relevance.note: Mid-point back-solve a=-1, b=0; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: In ΔPQR, S and T are points on PQ and PR respectively such that ST ∥ QR. If PS = 4 cm, PQ = 10 cm and PR = 15 cm, then PT is:
questions.explanation: By BPT, PS/PQ = PT/PR ⇒ 4/10 = PT/15 ⇒ PT = 6 cm.

relevance.note: BPT with whole side PQ: PT=6 with 9 trap

questions.question: ΔABC ~ ΔDEF and their perimeters are 30 cm and 18 cm respectively. If BC = 9 cm, then EF is:
questions.explanation: The ratio of perimeters of similar triangles equals the ratio of corresponding sides: BC/EF = 30/18 ⇒ EF = 9 × 18/30 = 5.4 cm.

relevance.note: Perimeter ratio = side ratio, EF=5.4 with 15 inverted trap

questions.question: In ΔABC, ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. In ΔPQR, ∠P = 50° and ∠R = 70°. Then:
questions.explanation: ∠C = 70° and ∠Q = 60°. So ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q and ∠C = ∠R, and by AA similarity ΔABC ~ ΔPQR.

relevance.note: Third angle 60° -> ΔABC ~ ΔPQR with wrong-order traps

questions.question: A boy 1.5 m tall stands 6 m away from the foot of a lamp-post and casts a shadow 2 m long on level ground. The height of the lamp-post is:
questions.explanation: The boy and the lamp-post form similar triangles with the tip of the shadow: 1.5/2 = h/(6 + 2) ⇒ h = 6 m.

relevance.note: Lamp-post similar triangles 6 m with 4.5 (ignoring distance) trap

questions.question: PA and PB are tangents drawn from an external point P to a circle. If ∠PAB = 65°, then ∠APB is:
questions.explanation: Tangents from an external point are equal, so PA = PB and ∠PBA = ∠PAB = 65°. Hence ∠APB = 180° − 130° = 50°.

relevance.note: Isosceles PAB -> ∠APB = 50° with 130 trap; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: A quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle. If AB = 6 cm, BC = 7 cm and CD = 4 cm, then AD is:
questions.explanation: For a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle, AB + CD = BC + AD ⇒ 6 + 4 = 7 + AD ⇒ AD = 3 cm.

relevance.note: Pitot property AD = 3; CBSE MCQ

questions.question:
Assertion (A): If PA and PB are tangents from an external point P to a circle with centre O, then the quadrilateral OAPB is cyclic.
Reason (R): In the quadrilateral OAPB, ∠OAP + ∠OBP = 180°.

Choose the correct option.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Each of ∠OAP and ∠OBP is 90° (radius ⟂ tangent), so their sum is 180°. A quadrilateral with a pair of opposite angles adding to 180° is cyclic. Both are true and R explains A.

relevance.note: OAPB cyclic since right angles at A,B; good CBSE A-R

questions.question: The value of (sin 45° + cos 45°)² is:

relevance.note: (sin45+cos45)^2 = 2; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: If 2 sin 2θ = √3 and 2θ is an acute angle, then θ is:

relevance.note: 2θ=60 -> θ=30 with 60 trap

questions.question: If sec θ = 13/12 and θ is acute, then tan θ is:

relevance.note: sec 13/12 -> tan 5/12 with 12/5 inverted trap

questions.question: (sec²θ − 1)(cosec²θ − 1) is equal to:
questions.explanation: sec²θ − 1 = tan²θ and cosec²θ − 1 = cot²θ. Their product tan²θ · cot²θ = 1.

relevance.note: tan²θ·cot²θ = 1; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: If sin θ + cos θ = √2, then the value of sin θ cos θ is:
questions.explanation: Squaring: sin²θ + cos²θ + 2 sin θ cos θ = 2 ⇒ 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ = 2 ⇒ sin θ cos θ = 1/2.

relevance.note: Square sinθ+cosθ=√2 -> product 1/2; CBSE MCQ

questions.question: From the top of a building 30 m high, the angle of depression of a car on the level ground is 30°. The distance of the car from the foot of the building is:
questions.explanation: The angle of elevation of the top from the car is also 30°. tan 30° = 30/d ⇒ d = 30√3 m.

relevance.note: Depression 30°, distance 30√3 with 10√3 trap

questions.question:
Assertion (A): sin θ = 4/3 for some acute angle θ.
Reason (R): In a right triangle the hypotenuse is the longest side, so for an acute angle θ, sin θ < 1.

Choose the correct option.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Since sin θ = opposite side/hypotenuse and the hypotenuse is the longest side, sin θ < 1 for an acute angle; R is true. Hence sin θ = 4/3 is impossible and A is false.

relevance.note: sin θ = 4/3 impossible; A false R true; CBSE A-R

questions.question: The perimeter of a sector of a circle of radius 7 cm with central angle 90° is (π = 22/7):
questions.explanation: Arc length = (90/360) × 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 11 cm. Perimeter = arc + two radii = 11 + 14 = 25 cm. (38.5 cm² is the area.)

relevance.note: Sector perimeter 2r + arc = 25 with arc-only 11 trap

questions.question: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm is (π = 22/7):
questions.explanation: TSA = 3πr² = 3 × 22/7 × 49 = 462 cm². (308 cm² is only the curved surface area 2πr².)

relevance.note: Hemisphere TSA 3πr² = 462 with CSA 308 trap

questions.question:
Assertion (A): If the radius of a sphere is doubled, its volume becomes 8 times the original volume.
Reason (R): The volume of a sphere of radius r is (4/3)πr³.

Choose the correct option.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Volume is proportional to r³, so doubling r multiplies the volume by 2³ = 8. Both are true and R explains A.

relevance.note: Volume scales 8× and formula explains; CBSE A-R

questions.topic: Statistics (Mean, Median, Mode of Grouped Data)
questions.question: For a distribution, the mode is 24 and the mean is 30. Using the empirical relation, the median is:
questions.explanation: 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean = 24 + 60 = 84 ⇒ Median = 28.

relevance.note: Median = (24+60)/3 = 28; CBSE empirical MCQ

questions.topic: Statistics (Mean, Median, Mode of Grouped Data)
questions.question: For the distribution 0–10 (f = 5), 10–20 (f = 8), 20–30 (f = 12), 30–40 (f = 10), 40–50 (f = 5), the median class is:
questions.explanation: N = 40, so N/2 = 20. Cumulative frequencies are 5, 13, 25, … The first cf greater than 20 is 25, so the median class is 20–30.

relevance.note: Median class via cf at N/2 = 20; CBSE MCQ

questions.topic: Statistics (Mean, Median, Mode of Grouped Data)
questions.question: For the distribution 10–20 (f = 4), 20–30 (f = 9), 30–40 (f = 15), 40–50 (f = 11), 50–60 (f = 6), the sum of the lower limits of the median class and the modal class is:
questions.explanation: N = 45, N/2 = 22.5; cumulative frequencies 4, 13, 28, … so the median class is 30–40. The highest frequency (15) also gives modal class 30–40. Sum of lower limits = 30 + 30 = 60.

questions.question: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled deck of 52 playing cards. The probability that it is a red king is:
questions.explanation: There are 2 red kings (hearts and diamonds). P = 2/52 = 1/26.

relevance.note: Red king 2/52 = 1/26 with 1/13 trap

questions.question:
Assertion (A): When a fair die is thrown once, the probability of getting a prime number is 1/2.
Reason (R): Every odd number on a die is a prime number.

Choose the correct option.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation: The primes on a die are 2, 3 and 5, so P = 3/6 = 1/2; A is true. 1 is odd but not prime, so R is false.

relevance.note: A true, R false (1 is not prime); good CBSE A-R trap

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the CBSE Class X Mathematics (Standard) board papers of 2024, 2025 and 2026 (all regional sets of Section A) and the CBSE sample papers for those sessions, as reproduced with solutions by Oswaal, Shaalaa and Collegedunia (found via WebSearch; the PDFs themselves could not be fetched in full, so set-level detail also relies on the writer's own knowledge of these papers). Section A always has 18 MCQs plus 2 Assertion–Reason items of 1 mark each. Only the rationalised NCERT syllabus is used (no areas of similar triangles, complementary-angle ratios, frustum or conversion of solids). Archetypes describe patterns in our own words; no board question is reproduced. Frequencies are per Section A (20 questions).
